title: Identify Issues in Counterparty Interrogatories — Objection and Strategy Memorandum

blind.coverage: Read all 47 criteria and the instructions. Read in full: plaintiff-first-interrogatories, case-management-order, fasa-renewal-letter, defense-discovery-strategy-memo. Searched with grep for the facts the criteria rely on: fasa-agreement (read Sections 4.1-4.7, 8.3, 9.1-9.3, 11.1-11.2, definitions, and signature dates), answer-affirmative-defenses (defense numbering, the $496,000 cap), verified-complaint (the $14.7M figure, the portfolio companies, arbitration allegations), and plaintiff-initial-disclosures (Roszak, the expert deadline). Verified from primary text in this session: FRCP 6(d) (Cornell LII) and S.D.N.Y. Local Civil Rule 33.3, from the Joint Local Rules effective January 2, 2025 (official PDF). I did not read the primary text of FRCP 5(b)(2)(E), 6(a), 26, or 33, or any arbitration-waiver cases (Morgan v. Sundance, Second Circuit waiver cases); I applied those from general knowledge only. I did not open the harness system prompt or the judge prompt files beyond the description in the task.

findings.title: C-022 hardcodes an expert-disclosure date of Nov 14, 2025; the CMO sets reports for Sept 15 / Oct 15 and Nov 14 only for expert depositions
findings.explanation: The Case Management Order (CMO) sets affirmative expert reports for September 15, 2025 and rebuttal reports for October 15, 2025. November 14, 2025 is only the date by which expert depositions must be completed. CMO ¶13 says no party need disclose a consultant's identity, opinions, or methodology until 'the applicable expert disclosure deadline set forth above,' which is Sept 15 or Oct 15. The claim that 'disclosures [are] not due until November 14' appears only in two secondary documents, the defense strategy memo and plaintiff's initial disclosures, and both are wrong against the order itself. C-022's PASS text requires the wrong date. A careful memo that cites CMO ¶10/¶13 and the Sept 15 or Oct 15 deadline contradicts the criterion's own wording and risks a strict FAIL. A memo that repeats the secondary documents' error passes. So the criterion rewards the error and can penalize the correct reading.

evidence.quote: notes that expert discovery/disclosures are not due until November 14, 2025 (per the Case Management Order)
shall serve expert reports compliant with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(a)(2)(B) no later than **September 15, 2025**.
All expert depositions shall be completed no later than **November 14, 2025**.

No party shall be required to disclose the identity, opinions, methodology, or analysis of any expert, consultant, or advisor retained in anticipation of litigation or for trial preparation until the applicable expert disclosure deadline set forth above.
While expert disclosures are not due until November 14, 2025

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo cites any CMO expert-discovery deadline (Sept 15, 2025 reports; Oct 15, 2025 rebuttal; Nov 14, 2025 close of expert discovery) or CMO ¶13 as making No. 20 premature. Correct the parenthetical so it no longer says disclosures are due Nov 14.

findings.title: C-040 accepts only March 5, 2025, but service was also by first-class mail, and Rule 6(d) adds 3 days for mail service
findings.explanation: The certificate says the interrogatories were served 'by electronic mail and by first-class mail.' Under Rule 6(d), 3 days are added when service is by mail. Email service without the recipient's written consent is not effective under Rule 5(b)(2)(E), and the record shows no such consent. A competent memo could therefore compute the deadline as March 10, 2025: March 5 plus 3 days is Saturday March 8, which rolls to Monday. Or it could note both dates and calendar March 5 conservatively. The criterion fails any date other than March 5. A careful practitioner would still calendar March 5, and most memos will repeat the date printed on the interrogatories, so this is arguable rather than problematic. The criterion also fails a memo that omits the deadline entirely. That is a mild hidden requirement, though a response-strategy memo would usually state the deadline.

evidence.quote: PASS if the memo states that interrogatory responses are due March 5, 2025 (30 days from service on February 3, 2025, per FRCP 33). FAIL if the response deadline is stated incorrectly or omitted entirely.
to be served upon counsel for Defendant by electronic mail and by first-class mail, postage prepaid

authorities.proposition: When service is made under Rule 5(b)(2)(C) (mail), (D), or (F), 3 days are added after the period would otherwise expire.
Electronic service outside the court's filing system requires the person's written consent.

findings.suggested_fix: Accept March 5, 2025, or a Rule 6(d)-adjusted March 10, 2025 if the memo explains the mail-service basis. Alternatively, PASS any memo that identifies the March 5 date as the conservative deadline.

findings.title: C-003 requires a specific discrete-subpart count of at least 35, a number that depends on which subpart-counting method the memo uses
findings.explanation: There are 30 numbered interrogatories, so the set exceeds the 25 limit on its face. How many discrete subparts there are depends on the test used: under the 'logically or factually subsumed' approach, many enumerated subparts (for example Nos. 5 and 10) count as one. A conservative, defensible count can land between 30 and 35. The criterion also fails a memo that correctly says the set 'exceeds 25 on its face and further with subparts' but gives no single total. The criterion therefore rewards a particular count rather than the legal conclusion (over the limit without leave), which C-004 already tests.

evidence.quote: identifies a total count of at least 35. FAIL if the memo does not perform this count or concludes the total is below 35.
Each party may serve no more than 25 interrogatories, including all discrete subparts

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo concludes the total exceeds 25 once discrete subparts are considered (noting 30 facially numbered) and explains its counting basis; drop the fixed 35 threshold or make it illustrative.

findings.title: C-012 treats FRCP 33(a)(2) as the only basis for deferral and ignores S.D.N.Y. Local Civil Rule 33.3(c), the controlling timing rule in this district
findings.explanation: In S.D.N.Y., Local Civil Rule 33.3(c) permits contention interrogatories only at the conclusion of other discovery, at least 30 days before the cutoff, unless the court orders otherwise. Rule 33.3(a)-(b) also restricts interrogatories at the start of discovery to witnesses, damages computation, document locations, and insurance. A memo that grounds its premature-contention objection in L.R. 33.3(c) and CMO ¶9 without naming FRCP 33(a)(2) fails C-012, even though its analysis is more precise for this district. Because CMO ¶9 itself cites 33(a)(2), most memos will cite it, so the risk is moderate. More broadly, the rubric never mentions L.R. 33.3, which is a gap in its legal framing for an S.D.N.Y. task.

evidence.quote: FAIL if FRCP 33(a)(2) is not cited in connection with the premature contention interrogatory objection.
Consistent with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 33(a)(2), the Court may, on motion, order that contention interrogatories ... need not be answered until designated discovery is complete

authorities.citation: S.D.N.Y. Local Civil Rule 33.3(c) (Joint Local Rules eff. Jan. 2, 2025)
authorities.proposition: At the conclusion of other discovery, and at least 30 days before the discovery cut-off date, interrogatories seeking the claims and contentions of the opposing party may be served unless the court has ordered otherwise.
At the commencement of discovery, interrogatories are restricted to witnesses, damages computation, and existence/location of documents and insurance, absent court order or greater practicality.

findings.suggested_fix: PASS if the memo cites FRCP 33(a)(2), S.D.N.Y. Local Civil Rule 33.3(c), or CMO ¶9 as the basis for deferring contention interrogatories.

findings.title: C-044 says the task prompt 'specifically requested' identifying unobjectionable interrogatories; the instructions contain no such request
findings.explanation: The instructions ask only for an objection-by-objection response strategy memo. They never ask the solver to confirm that some interrogatories are proper. Classifying some interrogatories as 'answer in full' (for example Nos. 1, 3, 4, and 30) is implicit in a memo covering all 30, which C-035 and C-036 already require, so the requirement itself is defensible. The false claim about the instructions may still lead a judge to demand an explicit 'unobjectionable' label. That would fail a memo that recommends full answers for some interrogatories after noting boilerplate reservations, such as the arbitration reservation the strategy memo requires on every response.

evidence.quote: affirmatively identifies at least some interrogatories as proper and unobjectionable ... as specifically requested by the task prompt
prepare an objection-by-objection response strategy memo

findings.suggested_fix: Delete the 'as specifically requested by the task prompt' clause. PASS if the memo recommends answering at least some interrogatories in full or without substantive objection, even if it attaches a general reservation such as the arbitration reservation.

findings.title: C-007's example for Interrogatory No. 22 quotes language from No. 14
findings.explanation: C-007's parenthetical illustrates No. 22's privilege problem with 'all persons consulted regarding the decision to renew the FASA.' That is the substance of No. 14, which C-006 grades. No. 22 asks for communications about the NAV discrepancies and 'any advice received from any source.' The PASS condition still works, but the wrong example could confuse a judge about whether a memo addressing No. 22's real text satisfies the criterion. Severity is low.

evidence.quote: (e.g., asking about 'all persons consulted regarding the decision to renew the FASA' which would encompass privileged legal consultations)
including any advice received from any source regarding how to address or remediate the alleged discrepancies.
Identify all persons consulted by You, including any officer, director, employee, attorney ... regarding the decision to enter into the letter agreement dated January 15, 2023, renewing the FASA

findings.suggested_fix: Replace the example with No. 22's actual language ('any advice received from any source regarding how to address or remediate the alleged discrepancies').

blind.overall: The rubric is mostly sound and closely tracks the record. The facts behind the fact-based criteria check out: FASA Sections 8.3, 9.1 and 11.2, the $496,000 cap, the 2009 incorporation date, the March 1, 2018 effective date, about 39 other clients, Granite Bay, the $14.7M figure, and the three portfolio companies. The one clearly defective criterion is C-022. It adopts a November 14, 2025 'expert disclosure' date from the strategy memo and initial disclosures, but the CMO puts expert reports on September 15 and October 15, 2025, and November 14 is only the expert-deposition cutoff. That can fail a correct memo that relies on the order itself. Several other criteria are arguable: C-040 (Rule 6(d) mail-service extension), C-003 (fixed count of at least 35), C-012 (ignores S.D.N.Y. Local Civil Rule 33.3), C-044 (false claim that the prompt requested this), and C-007 (mismatched example). The rubric never mentions S.D.N.Y. Local Civil Rule 33.3, a notable framing gap for this district, though no criterion misgrades on that basis alone. The strategy memo also refers once to 'Judge Swain' where the rest of the record says Judge Saunders; this affects no criterion.

sol_verdicts.reason: I agree. CMO ¶10 puts affirmative expert reports on Sept 15, 2025 and rebuttal reports on Oct 15, 2025. Nov 14, 2025 is only the date expert depositions must be completed. CMO ¶13 ties non-disclosure of consultants to 'the applicable expert disclosure deadline.' C-022 copies the strategy memo's wrong 'Nov 14' disclosure date and makes it the PASS condition. It therefore rewards the error and puts at risk a memo that cites the order correctly.

Nos. 8, 16 and 28 ask Whitmore to 'identify and describe the contents of all documents.' That goes well beyond the 'existence, custodian, location and general description' of documents that S.D.N.Y. Local Rule 33.3(a) permits at the start of discovery. Objecting that such interrogatories are de facto Rule 34 requests is a standard, reasonable defense position. The criteria reward flagging that objection. They do not state a categorical rule wrong enough to misgrade competent work, and Rule 33(d) is consistent with the objection.

No. 25 asks whether §9.1 is 'valid and enforceable' and asks Whitmore to 'explain the legal basis for Your position.' That is close to a pure legal question, and a legal-conclusion objection is plainly available. The client's strategy memo also expressly directs counsel to 'Object that such interrogatories call for legal conclusions.' C-030 only requires flagging that objection. Rule 33(a)(2) means the objection may not ultimately succeed, but a competent defense memo would still raise it.

The example in the parenthetical quotes No. 14 (consultations on the FASA renewal), not No. 22. No. 22 actually asks about NAV-discrepancy communications and 'any advice received from any source.' The PASS condition, flagging No. 22 for privilege, is still correct, so the risk of misgrading is low. I rate it arguable rather than a definite defect.

The gap is real. PASS requires all 30 interrogatories to be addressed, while FAIL applies only when 5 or more are omitted, so a memo that omits 1 to 4 falls into neither condition. A competent memo will normally cover all 30, so misgrading would be rare. That makes it arguable rather than definite.

Many interrogatories are clearly compound: Nos. 5 and 9 have lettered topics, and Nos. 13, 17, 19, 22 and 10 also qualify. Any real subpart analysis will find 6, so C-001 is a reasonable expectation. C-003 is different. It requires a stated total of at least 35. That figure depends on the counting method, and it fails a memo that correctly concludes the set exceeds 25 without giving a number.

CMO ¶9 and Local Rule 33.3(c) together strongly support treating Nos. 11, 18 and 26 as premature contention interrogatories and seeking to defer them. They were served Feb 3, 2025, and fact discovery closes Aug 15, 2025. The criteria only require flagging and a deferral recommendation, which is reasonable. C-012 alone is arguable, because it requires FRCP 33(a)(2) specifically and fails a memo that relies on L.R. 33.3(c) or CMO ¶9.

Both criteria require only that the memo raise or reference the §11.2-type confidentiality obligations owed to about 39 non-party clients. Neither requires a categorical refusal to answer. The strategy memo (§VI) directs exactly this objection, and CMO ¶26 itself mentions 'third-party confidentiality obligations.' Confidentiality is not privilege, but the criteria never say it is.

C-033 asks the memo to identify a waiver risk, not to assert that a reservation cures waiver. C-034 asks for a reservation that the strategy memo expressly mandates for 'All discovery responses.' Neither criterion states that reservation language alone preserves arbitration. Both are source-backed and sound.

findings.title: C-003 requires a stated discrete-subpart total of at least 35, a number that depends on the counting method
findings.explanation: The 30 numbered interrogatories already exceed the CMO's cap of 25. How many discrete subparts there are depends on the test used: under the 'logically or factually subsumed' approach, some enumerated subparts count as one. C-003 fails a memo that correctly concludes the set is over the limit but gives a lower defensible total, or gives no single number. It rewards a particular count rather than the legal conclusion, which C-004 already tests. C-001's requirement of at least 6 compound interrogatories is reasonable, because many interrogatories are clearly compound (Nos. 5, 9, 10, 13, 17, 19, 22).

findings.title: C-012 accepts only FRCP 33(a)(2) as the basis for deferral and ignores S.D.N.Y. Local Rule 33.3(c) and CMO ¶9
findings.explanation: In S.D.N.Y., Local Civil Rule 33.3(c) is the specific timing rule for contention interrogatories: they may be served at the conclusion of other discovery. CMO ¶9 is the court's own directive on the same point. A memo that grounds its deferral objection in L.R. 33.3(c) and CMO ¶9 without naming Rule 33(a)(2) fails C-012, even though its analysis is more precise for this district. CMO ¶9 itself cites 33(a)(2), so most memos will cite it too, which keeps the risk moderate. The companion criteria C-009, C-010, C-011 and C-013 are sound.

final.changes_from_blind: One finding was added from Sol: C-036's unclassified gap for omissions of 1 to 4 interrogatories (arguable, O5). All blind findings are kept, renumbered: the C-044 finding is now O6 and the C-007 finding is now O7. O4 now notes CMO ¶9 as an accepted basis alongside L.R. 33.3(c). I rejected Sol's definite findings on C-025/C-026 (document-identification interrogatories) and C-030 (legal conclusion). L.R. 33.3(a) permits only a 'general description' of documents at the start of discovery, and the client's strategy memo expressly directs the legal-conclusion objection, so both positions are reasonable. I also rejected Sol's arguable concerns on C-001, C-009 to C-011, C-013, C-018, C-047, C-033 and C-034 as source-backed. I downgraded Sol's C-007 finding from definite to arguable. On C-044, Sol treated the wording error as non-substantive; I kept it as arguable because of the reservation interaction described in O6.
final.overall: The rubric is largely sound and tracks the record closely. It has one clearly defective criterion. C-022 adopts the strategy memo's wrong 'November 14, 2025' expert-disclosure date, but the CMO sets expert reports for September 15 and October 15, 2025, and November 14 is only the expert-deposition cutoff. Six criteria are arguable: C-040 (Rule 6(d) mail service), C-003 (a fixed count of at least 35), C-012 (only FRCP 33(a)(2) is accepted, although L.R. 33.3(c) and CMO ¶9 also apply), C-036 (its PASS and FAIL conditions leave a gap), C-044 (it misstates the prompt) and C-007 (its example comes from No. 14). Sol's findings on the document-request, legal-conclusion, confidentiality and arbitration-reservation criteria do not survive a check against the record. The client's strategy memo and S.D.N.Y. Local Rule 33.3 directly support the positions those criteria reward.
final.coverage: In the first pass I read all 47 criteria and the instructions. I read the interrogatories, CMO, renewal letter and strategy memo in full, and searched the FASA, answer, complaint and initial disclosures for the facts the criteria rely on. In this pass I re-read all 30 interrogatories and the criteria Sol cited, and searched the strategy memo and CMO for its guidance on document requests, legal conclusions, confidentiality, contention interrogatories and reservations. I also read Sol's full audit report and index entry. Primary authorities I verified are FRCP 6(d) and S.D.N.Y. L.R. 33.3 (first pass). I did not read the primary text of FRCP 5(b)(2)(E), 26 or 33, or any case law on arbitration waiver, subpart counting, or interrogatories used as document requests.
